scenes.title: Cold open
narration: In 1928, Bascom Lamar Lunsford organized Asheville's Mountain Dance and Folk Festival, where team clogging officially took root.
This is Clogging. 20th century.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (NMA5kgajhEA)
Title card: Clogging · United States · 20th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: In the United States, team clogging originated from square dance teams at Asheville, North Carolina's Mountain Dance and Folk Festival in 1928, organized by Bascom Lamar Lunsford.
The Soco Gap Dancers performed at the White House in 1939, causing an uptick in popularity.

The dance developed primarily from the interaction between Irish Sean-nós step dancing and Black American buck dancing, with additional influences from English, Scottish, German, and Cherokee step dances.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Clogging is performed at folk festivals, fairs, and community gatherings to bring people together for socialization.
It is practiced both as a social activity and a competitive sport where teams vie for money and trophies.
It holds official state dance status in Kentucky and North Carolina.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Reading Clog & Step Dance Festival Performers' Show 1990 (https://archive.org/details/ReadingClogStepDanceFestivalPerformersShow1990)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers use their footwear percussively by striking the heel, the toe, or both against a floor or each other to create audible rhythms, usually keeping the downbeat with the heel.
Unlike tap dancers who use arm movements and stage presence, cloggers limit the movement of their upper body and focus intensely on rapid footwork.
Categories include shuffle clogging, clogging en cadence, rhythmic clogging, stomp clogging, and buck-dancing.
Watch for shuffle clogging, stomp clogging.

Captions name each signature move as it appears

scenes.title: Listen
narration: American clogging is associated with old-time music, which relies on Anglo-Celtic fiddle tunes by white Appalachians as well as Affrilachian banjo tunes, as well as modern bluegrass music.
Live music at festivals and community events drives the percussive footwork.
Listen for the fiddle, banjo.
Old-time and bluegrass tunes driven by Anglo-Celtic fiddle melodies and Affrilachian banjo playing, underscored by the continuous percussive clatter of footwear hitting a wooden floor.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Many traditional shoes lacked metal points, using leather and velvet with wooden or hard leather soles, while modern or variant styles incorporate jingle-taps with loose metal plates.
The dance is performed at old-time and bluegrass music festivals, community fairs, logging camps, and square dances.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Bascom Lamar Lunsford organized the 1928 Mountain Dance and Folk Festival in Asheville.
William Henry Lane is noted as an influential dancer who integrated the style.
Minor regional differences in style appear across Appalachian communities, including local names like buck dancing, hoedowning, back stopping, flat footing, or clogging.
Clogging evolved from Irish Sean-nós step dancing, Black American buck dancing, and European step dances, and it directly gave rise to modern tap dance.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Clogging is child of Tap dance: American clogging served as the direct evolutionary ancestor to modern tap dance.
Clogging is parent of Sean-nós dance: Irish Sean-nós step dancing was a primary foundational influence on American clogging.
